book.title: Yunus Emre: Faith, Character, and Poetry (A2)

pages.title: Yunus Emre
pages.content:
Yunus Emre was one of the first great Anatolian Turkish poets. He was born in 1240 in Anatolia. People could easily understand his poems because he wrote and said them in simple Turkish. He helped improve the Turkish language. His poems have important moral lessons. These lessons are still very important for Turkish culture today. He also spoke of the greatness and oneness of Allah, love for Allah and Prophet Muhammad (pbuh).

At that time, schools were called madrasas. After he completed his madrasa education, he followed the way of the dervishes and became a dervish. Dervishes trained to be good people with moral values under the guidance of a teacher at dervish houses.

Yunus Emre became a dervish pupil of Taptuk Emre. He traveled to many cities in Anatolia, as well as Syria and Azerbaijan. He lived in the same period as Mevlana. Mevlana died in 1273 and later Yunus passed away in 1320. Yunus was 33 or 34 years old when Mevlana died.

languageFocusExercises.title: Past Forms in a Life Story
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each verb with its past form from Chapter 1.
languageFocusExercises.question: What is the past form of each verb?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A life story tells finished events, so Chapter 1 uses past forms. These four verbs are irregular: they do not take -ed. “He became a dervish.” “He wrote and said them in simple Turkish.” “He also spoke of the greatness and oneness of Allah.”

feedback.correct: Good. You know the irregular past forms in Yunus Emre’s life story.
feedback.incorrect: Look at Chapter 1 again. Find “became”, “wrote”, “said” and “spoke”. They do not end in -ed.

languageFocusExercises.title: Because, After, When
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Fill each gap from the word bank. Two words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which word gives a reason, an order or a time?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: People could easily understand his poems [blank] he … them in simple Turkish. … [blank] he completed his madrasa education, he followed the way of the dervishes … Yunus was 33 or 34 years old [blank] Mevlana died.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Because” gives a reason: people understood his poems because he used simple Turkish. “After” shows the order of events: First his madrasa education, then the dervish way. “When” links a fact to a time: Yunus was 33 or 34 at the time Mevlana died.

feedback.correct: Correct. You used because for a reason, after for the order of events and when for a time.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first and last paragraphs of Chapter 1 again. Ask: Is it a reason? Is it the next event? Is it a time?

pages.title: Our Dervish Yunus
pages.content:
Dervishes tried to find Allah everywhere not only with their eyes but also with their hearts. They witnessed the signs of Allah in the whole universe. They shared these experiences about Allah with other people. Dervishes were fully aware that they were in need of Allah in every way. That is why, even if they were rich, they always called themselves poor. If they were wealthy, their wealth was not in their hearts, but in their hands to give to charity. They shared what they had with the needy; they could call themselves poor, but their hearts were very rich. Dervishes were generous-hearted and open-handed.

Because of the Creator, they forgave and tolerated others. They were kind and cheerful; they were not cold or sulky. They tried to understand everyone and found a solution to their problems. They always tried to leave bad habits like jealousy, arrogance, stinginess, greediness, selfishness, or gossiping.

vocabulary.definition: Saw or felt something clearly.
Everything that exists.
Help given to people in need.
Unhappy and unfriendly in silence.

hotspots.title: Hearts and Eyes
hotspots.description: Dervishes tried to find Allah everywhere not only with their eyes but also with their hearts.

hotspots.title: The Needy
hotspots.description: They shared what they had with the needy.

exercises.title: Wealth in the Hand
exercises.instructions: Is the sentence true or false? Use Chapter 2.
exercises.question: When the dervishes were rich, they kept their money for themselves.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 2 says their wealth was “not in their hearts, but in their hands to give to charity.” It also says, “They shared what they had with the needy.”

feedback.correct: Correct! The dervishes did not keep their wealth. They shared it with people in need.
feedback.incorrect: Read the end of the first paragraph again. What did the dervishes do with what they had?

languageFocusExercises.title: Why Did They Say “Poor”?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentences from Chapter 2. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Dervishes were fully aware that they were in need of Allah in every way. That is why, even if they were rich, they always called themselves poor.” Why did the dervishes call themselves poor?
options: They knew that they needed Allah in every way.
They wanted people to give them charity.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “That is why” points back to the sentence before it. That sentence gives the reason: they knew they needed Allah. “Even if they were rich” means: Also at times when they had money. So “poor” here is not about money.

feedback.correct: Correct. “That is why” points back to the reason: they needed Allah in every way.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the sentence before “That is why”. It gives the reason. And “even if they were rich” tells us they sometimes had money.

languageFocusExercises.title: But, Because Of, Were Not
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct words for each sentence from Chapter 2.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which words fit the sentences about the dervishes?

formChoices.sentence: If they were wealthy, their wealth was not in their hearts, [choice] in their hands to give to charity.
[choice] the Creator, they forgave and tolerated others.
They were kind and cheerful; they [choice] cold or sulky.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Not … but …” takes away one idea and gives the right one: Not in their hearts, but in their hands. “Because of” comes before a noun (“because of the Creator”); “because” needs a full sentence after it. With an adjective in the past, use “were not”: “they were not cold or sulky”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You chose the right linking word and the right past form.
feedback.incorrect: Read Chapter 2 again. Is there a noun after the gap or a full sentence? Is the word after the gap an adjective (cold, sulky)?

languageFocusExercises.question: What were the dervishes like?

feedback.correct: Use accurate Chapter 2 language to describe character, action and contrast.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Add “but” or a reason: “They called themselves poor, but …”

pages.title: The Difficult Path
pages.content:
They followed honesty, patience, humility, generosity, respect and trust in Allah.

In fact, the path of dervishhood was a very difficult one. Yunus Emre beautifully makes this point in his poem that begins with the words, “You cannot be a dervish.”

[POEM_GRID]
[POEM]
English:
A dervish needs a wounded heart.
He needs eyes full of tears.
He needs to be as easy going as a sheep.
You can’t be a dervish.
Turkish:
Derviş bağrı baş gerek
Gözü dolu yaş gerek
Koyundan yavaş gerek
Sen derviş olamazsın
[/POEM]
[POEM]
English:
He must be without hands when someone hits him.
He must be tongueless when people make fun of him.
A dervish needs to be without any desires (selfless).
You can’t be a dervish.
Turkish:
Dövene elsiz gerek
Sövene dilsiz gerek
Derviş gönülsüz gerek
Sen derviş olamazsın
[/POEM]
[/POEM_GRID]

Dervishes had a way of life of their own. They ate less, spoke less, slept less, and spent their time on useful activities. Dervishes lived a moderate and disciplined life according to Islam.

Yunus Emre was one of these dervishes. He received his dervish training at the school of his master, Taptuk Emre.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:yunus-yunus-emre
__historical_entity__:yunus-taptuk-emre
Staying calm while waiting or facing difficulty.
Being happy to give to others.
Not too much and not too little.
Following clear rules and a fixed order every day.

hotspots.title: Path of Dervishhood

exercises.title: A Way of Life
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer from Chapter 3.
exercises.question: The dervishes had a way of life of their own. How did they live?
options: They spent all their days at the madrasa.
They ate less, spoke less and slept less.
They ate more and slept more than other people.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 3 says: “They ate less, spoke less, slept less, and spent their time on useful activities.” It calls this “a moderate and disciplined life according to Islam.”

feedback.correct: Yes! They ate, spoke and slept less, and they used their time well. This was a disciplined life.
feedback.incorrect: Read the paragraph after the poem again. Find the sentence after “a way of life of their own”.

languageFocusExercises.title: What Does the Poem Mean?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each line of the poem with its meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: What does a dervish need, and what must he do?

matchingPairs.left: He needs to be as easy going as a sheep.
matchingPairs.right: He is calm and gentle with everyone.

matchingPairs.left: He must be without hands when someone hits him.
He must be tongueless when people make fun of him.
matchingPairs.right: He says nothing back to rude people.

matchingPairs.left: A dervish needs to be without any desires (selfless).

He is calm and gentle with everyone.
correctAnswer.He must be tongueless when people make f: He says nothing back to rude people.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The poem uses pictures, not real body parts: “without hands” means he does not hit back, and “tongueless” means he does not answer rude words. “Needs to” and “must” tell us what is necessary for a dervish. The last line of each verse, “You can’t be a dervish”, says that this path is very hard.

feedback.correct: Good. You understood the pictures in the poem.
feedback.incorrect: Read the poem again. Ask: What does a person “without hands” not do? What does a “tongueless” person not do?

languageFocusExercises.title: Ate, Slept, Spent
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct past form for each sentence.
languageFocusExercises.question: How did the dervishes live?

formChoices.sentence: Dervishes had a way of life of their own. They [choice] less, …
… and [choice] their time on useful activities.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Eat”, “sleep” and “spend” are irregular verbs. Their past forms are “ate”, “slept” and “spent”, not “eated”, “sleeped” or “spended”. With “less”, the sentence shows a simple, disciplined life.

feedback.correct: Correct. You used the irregular past forms.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the paragraph after the poem in Chapter 3. These verbs do not take -ed in the past.

pages.title: The Woodcutter Yunus
pages.content:
He became a student of Taptuk Emre at a young age. In Taptuk Emre’s dervish house, the first condition to be a student was to be humble and willing to serve people and all creatures.

This was also the case for Yunus. He told his master, “I will do whatever service you ask of me.” Taptuk then assigned Yunus to the wood-cutting duties at the dervish house. Some jobs look ordinary at first glance. The primary goal is to break the ego and give up bad habits.

There was a mountain behind Taptuk’s dervish house. Taptuk asked Yunus to collect wood from the mountain. Every day, Yunus carried wood on his back from the mountain. But he never cut or brought green or crooked wood. He always said, “Crooked wood cannot go into the dervish house.”

__historical_entity__:yunus-yunus-emre
__historical_entity__:yunus-taptuk-emre
Not proud; respectful and modest.
Work done to help others.

hotspots.title: Wood-Cutting Duties
hotspots.description: Taptuk then assigned Yunus to the wood-cutting duties at the dervish house.

hotspots.title: Crooked Wood
hotspots.description: Yunus never cut or brought green or crooked wood.

exercises.title: Yunus the Woodcutter
exercises.instructions: Put the events from Chapter 4 in the right order.
exercises.question: What happened first, next and last?

sequencingItems.text: Yunus became a student of Taptuk Emre at a young age.
Yunus said, “I will do whatever service you ask of me.”
Taptuk gave Yunus the wood-cutting duties.
Every day, Yunus carried wood on his back from the mountain.

exercises.explanation: First Yunus became Taptuk Emre’s student. Then he told his master, “I will do whatever service you ask of me.” After that, Taptuk “assigned Yunus to the wood-cutting duties”, and every day Yunus carried wood from the mountain.

feedback.correct: Great! Yunus was humble: He promised to serve, and then he did his work every day.
feedback.incorrect: Read Chapter 4 from the beginning to the end. Find what Yunus said, what Taptuk asked and what Yunus did every day.

languageFocusExercises.title: How Often?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 4. True or false?
languageFocusExercises.question: “But he never cut or brought green or crooked wood.” — Statement: Yunus sometimes brought crooked wood to the dervish house.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Never” means “not one time”. So Yunus did not bring crooked wood at any time. Chapter 4 also uses “every day” (a daily action) and “always” (at all times) to show Yunus’s routine.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Never” means not one time, so the statement is false.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the word “never” in the sentence. Does it mean “sometimes” or “not one time”?

languageFocusExercises.title: A Promise and a Routine
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Fill each gap from the word bank. Two words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: What did Yunus promise, and how did he work?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: He told his master, “I [blank] do whatever service you ask of me.” … Taptuk asked Yunus [blank] collect wood from the mountain. [blank] day, Yunus carried wood on his back from the mountain. … He [blank] said, “Crooked wood cannot go into the dervish house.”
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “I will …” makes a promise. “Asked + person + to + verb” tells us what someone asked another person to do: “asked Yunus to collect wood”. “Every day” is a daily action, and “always” means at all times. Learners often say “I am do” or “asked him for collect”, but English needs “I will do” and “asked him to collect”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You completed the promise, the request and the routine.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second and third paragraphs of Chapter 4 again. After “asked Yunus”, which small word comes before “collect”?

languageFocusExercises.title: Say It: Service and Routine
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Say three short sentences about how Yunus served.
languageFocusExercises.question: How did Yunus serve his teacher?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong A2 response moves from language noticed in the chapter to a short spoken description of Yunus’s behavior.

feedback.correct: Use one sentence about willingness, one about his promise, and one about his daily routine.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Say he was ready: “Yunus was willing to …”
discussionPrompts.example: Yunus was willing to serve people and all creatures.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Give his promise: “He said, ‘I will …’”
discussionPrompts.example: He said, “I will do whatever service you ask of me.”

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Say what he did every day: “Every day he …, but he never …”
discussionPrompts.example: Every day he carried wood from the mountain, but he never brought crooked wood.

beforeYouRead.question: Guess first: What was behind Taptuk’s dervish house?
beforeYouRead.quote: There was a mountain behind Taptuk’s dervish house.

pages.title: Straight Wood and the Ego
pages.content:
Just imagine! Carrying firewood every day hurts your back and leaves bad cuts. He chose the straightest pieces of wood with the greatest care. So why was he doing that?

The wood was like Yunus’s ego, and it looked like it needed to be corrected. It looked like Yunus was working with wood to fix crooked pieces. But in fact, he was training his own heart and ego. Every time he used the axe, he made a bad part of himself better. This service taught him how to have a good heart and do the right thing.

Yunus served his teacher Taptuk Emre in this way for exactly forty years. Taptuk Emre noticed that Yunus never carried crooked wood to the house. One day he asked Yunus the following question:

“My Yunus, is there no crooked wood in the mountains? Why do you always bring straight pieces?”

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:yunus-yunus-emre
__historical_entity__:yunus-taptuk-emre
Close attention so that you do something well.
The part of a person that can become proud or selfish.
Made right or better.
A tool used to cut wood.

hotspots.title: Straightest Pieces
hotspots.description: He chose the straightest pieces of wood with the greatest care.

hotspots.title: Heart and Ego

exercises.title: Straight Wood
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer from Chapter 5.
exercises.question: Why did Yunus choose only the straightest pieces of wood?
options: Straight wood was easier to carry down the mountain.
He was training his own heart and ego.
Taptuk Emre promised him a gift for it.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 5 asks, “So why was he doing that?” Then it says: “It looked like Yunus was working with wood to fix crooked pieces. But in fact, he was training his own heart and ego.”

feedback.correct: Right! The wood is like Yunus’s ego. Every time he used the axe, he made a bad part of himself better.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 5 again. Find the words “But in fact …”.

languageFocusExercises.title: From “It Looked Like” to “In Fact”
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Put the sentences from Chapter 5 in order.
languageFocusExercises.question: What did it look like, and what was really happening?

sequencingItems.text: It looked like Yunus was working with wood to fix crooked pieces.
But in fact, he was training his own heart and ego.
Every time he used the axe, he made a bad part of himself better.
This service taught him how to have a good heart and do the right thing.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “It looked like …” gives a first idea: What we see. “But in fact …” gives the true meaning. “Every time …” shows something that happens again and again. “This service taught him how to …” gives the result: What Yunus learned.

feedback.correct: Correct. You followed the chapter from the first idea to the true meaning and the result.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 5. Start with “It looked like”. Which sentence says what is true “in fact”?

languageFocusExercises.title: Build Taptuk’s Question
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Put the words in order to make Taptuk’s question.
languageFocusExercises.question: What did Taptuk ask Yunus?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: To ask about a habit, use: Why + do + you + (always) + verb … ? “Always” comes before the main verb: “Why do you always bring straight pieces?” The other question, “Is there no crooked wood in the mountains?”, starts with “Is there” to ask if something exists.

feedback.correct: Well done. You built the question in the right order.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the last line of Chapter 5. Start with “Why”, then “do you”. “Always” goes before “bring”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Say It: What the Work Really Means
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Say four short sentences about what Yunus’s work really meant.
languageFocusExercises.question: What was Yunus really learning?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong A2 response uses the chapter’s own discourse pattern: first impression, deeper reality, repeated action and learning.

feedback.correct: Use the four sentence starters to explain the chapter’s deeper meaning clearly.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Say what he learned: “This service taught him how to …”

pages.title: The Door of Honesty
pages.content:
Yunus replied, “My teacher, this place is a door of honesty and goodness. Not even a crooked piece of wood can enter here. And a dishonest and insincere person cannot enter this place, either.”

Nature and living alone helped the dervish think deeply about himself. During this time, Yunus made his heart purer. He learned the special language of all creatures. He looked at nature and found a lesson from everything in it, like reading the Qur’an. Also, the lessons and talks at the dervish house helped him with this learning. For Yunus, woodcutting in nature helped him become a better person.

He first learned to be alone with Allah in the mountains. The mountains are quiet and far from people. There are trees, animals, and rivers. If you look closely, you find a deeper meaning in everything in nature. Everything tells a story.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:yunus-tekke
__historical_entity__:yunus-yunus-emre
Telling the truth and doing what is right.
The quality of being kind and doing right.
Living things, such as people and animals, made by Allah.
Cleaner and freer from anything bad.

hotspots.title: Honesty and Goodness
hotspots.description: Yunus said that the dervish house was a door of honesty and goodness.

hotspots.title: Lessons from Nature

exercises.title: Who Can Enter?
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer from Chapter 6.
exercises.question: Yunus says that a crooked piece of wood cannot enter the dervish house. Who else cannot enter?
exercises.explanation: Yunus answers Taptuk: “this place is a door of honesty and goodness. Not even a crooked piece of wood can enter here. And a dishonest and insincere person cannot enter this place, either.”

feedback.correct: Yes! Crooked wood and a dishonest person cannot enter. The dervish house is a place of honesty and goodness.
feedback.incorrect: Read Yunus’s answer at the beginning of Chapter 6 again. Find the word “either”.

languageFocusExercises.title: If You Look Closely
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match the beginnings and endings from the end of Chapter 6.
languageFocusExercises.question: What are the mountains like, and what can you find?

matchingPairs.right: you find a deeper meaning in everything in nature.

correctAnswer.If you look closely,: you find a deeper meaning in everything in nature.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Are” + adjectives describes a place (quiet, far from people). “There are” + plural nouns says what is in a place. “If you look closely, you find …” has two parts: First what you do, then what happens. “Everything” is singular, so the verb takes -s: “tells”.

feedback.correct: Good. You rebuilt the sentences about the mountains.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 6. Which ending is a list of things? Which ending starts with “you find”?

languageFocusExercises.title: Helped Him Think, Made It Purer
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Fill each gap from the word bank. Two words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: What comes after “helped the dervish”, “made his heart” and “learned”?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: Nature and living alone helped the dervish [blank] deeply about himself. During this time, Yunus made his heart [blank]. … He first learned [blank] alone with Allah in the mountains.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: After “help + person”, use the base verb: “helped the dervish think”. “Make + thing + adjective” shows a change: “made his heart purer” (more pure than before). After “learn”, use “to + verb”: “learned to be alone”.

feedback.correct: Correct. You used the right form after helped, made and learned.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second and third paragraphs of Chapter 6 again. We say “helped him think”, not “helped him thinking”, and “learned to be”, not “learned being”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Say It: Learning from a Place
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Say four short sentences about how nature helped Yunus.
languageFocusExercises.question: How did the mountains help Yunus learn?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong A2 response combines description, help/change language and the chapter’s simple if-result pattern.

feedback.correct: Use the chapter’s own language to connect place, learning and discovery.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Describe the place: “The mountains were … and …”

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Say how nature helped: “Nature helped Yunus …”

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Say what he learned: “He learned to …”

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Say what you can find: “If you look closely, you …”
discussionPrompts.example: If you look closely, you find a deeper meaning in everything in nature.

pages.title: A Single Daisy
pages.content:
One day, Taptuk Emre said to his students, “Today, all of you go up the mountain and bring me flowers. I will give a gift to whoever prepares the most beautiful bunch of flowers.” All the dervishes went out into the fields. They picked flowers and ran back to their teacher. Yunus was the last to return.

In the late afternoon, he returned with a single daisy. Some dervishes were making fun of Yunus. They whispered in each other’s ears, “Just look at him! All he could find was a single daisy!” Taptuk asked Yunus about the meaning behind this single daisy. Yunus replied, “My teacher, I walked around the fields, and wherever I saw a flower, I heard that it was saying the name of Allah. I could not cut any of them.”

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:yunus-yunus-emre
__historical_entity__:yunus-taptuk-emre
A group of flowers held together.
A small white flower with a yellow middle.
Laughing at someone in an unkind way.
Spoke very quietly.

hotspots.title: Only One Flower
hotspots.description: In the late afternoon, Yunus returned with a single daisy.

hotspots.title: The Name of Allah
hotspots.description: Yunus heard every flower he saw saying the name of Allah.

exercises.title: A Single Daisy
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer from Chapter 7.
exercises.question: Why did Yunus not bring a big bunch of flowers?
options: The other dervishes picked all the flowers first.
Every flower he saw was saying the name of Allah.
Taptuk Emre asked each student for only one flower.
exercises.explanation: Yunus tells Taptuk: “wherever I saw a flower, I heard that it was saying the name of Allah. I could not cut any of them.”

feedback.correct: Right! Yunus heard the flowers remembering Allah, so he could not cut them.
feedback.incorrect: Read Yunus’s answer to Taptuk at the end of Chapter 7. Find the words “wherever I saw a flower …”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Tell the Flower Story in Order
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Put the sentences from Chapter 7 in order.
languageFocusExercises.question: What happened first, next and last?

sequencingItems.text: One day, Taptuk Emre said to his students, “Today, all of you go up the mountain and bring me flowers.”
The students picked flowers and ran back to their teacher.
Yunus was the last to return.
The students whispered in each other’s ears, “Just look at him! …”
Yunus replied, “My teacher, I walked around the fields, …”

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “One day” starts a story. Then the dervishes pick flowers and come back; Yunus comes back last, “in the late afternoon”. Some dervishes laugh at him, Taptuk asks about the daisy, and Yunus answers.

feedback.correct: Correct. You told the story in the right order.
feedback.incorrect: Read Chapter 7 again. Start with “One day”. Who comes back first: The other dervishes or Yunus?

languageFocusExercises.title: Some, Any, A Single
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct word for each sentence from Chapter 7.
languageFocusExercises.question: How many dervishes? How many flowers?

formChoices.sentence: [choice] dervishes were making fun of Yunus.
“Just look at him! All he could find was [choice] daisy!”
I could not cut [choice] of them.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Some” means part of a group, not everyone: some dervishes laughed. “A single” means only one: a single daisy. After “not”, use “any”: “I could not cut any of them” means he cut not one flower. “Could not … none” is a double negative, so it is wrong.

feedback.correct: Well done. You used some, a single and any correctly.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 7. Did all the dervishes laugh, or only part of the group? Which word comes after “not”?

languageFocusExercises.title: Say It: Retell the Daisy Scene
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Retell Chapter 7 in four short sentences.
languageFocusExercises.question: What happened with the flowers?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong A2 retelling uses a clear event order and simple expressions such as all, some, a single, could not, and when.

feedback.correct: Use the sentence starters to keep the story clear and in order.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Start the story: “One day, Taptuk asked all the students to …”
discussionPrompts.example: One day, Taptuk asked all the students to bring him flowers from the mountain.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Compare Yunus with the others: “The dervishes …, but Yunus …”
discussionPrompts.example: The dervishes ran back with many flowers, but Yunus came back last with a single daisy.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Give his reason: “He could not cut any flowers because …”
discussionPrompts.example: He could not cut any flowers because he heard them saying the name of Allah.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Say how it ends: “When it started to get dark, …”
discussionPrompts.example: When it started to get dark, a daisy called out to Yunus.

beforeYouRead.question: Guess first: When did Yunus come back?
beforeYouRead.quote: In the late afternoon, he returned with a single daisy.

iCan: I can tell the story of the single daisy.
I can say how many people or things there were.
I can retell a short story in the right order.

pages.title: A Meaningful Life
pages.content:
“When it started to get dark, a daisy called out to me: ‘Come, dervish Yunus. My time is up now; I’m dried up and dying. At least pick me and let my life end in the hands of a dervish.’”

In these two stories, Yunus tells us to always remember Allah in our hearts and to do every job well. He says that we must always do our best when we work. Every job is important, so we should do it well and correctly for the love of Allah. Our hearts must be full of love for Him during our daily lives. This helps us live a meaningful and fruitful life.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:yunus-yunus-emre
No longer fresh because it has lost water.
Coming to the end of life.
Having an important purpose or value.
Useful and successful.

hotspots.title: The Daisy’s Words
hotspots.description: The daisy said, “My time is up now; I’m dried up and dying.”

hotspots.title: A Fruitful Life
hotspots.description: Remembering Allah and doing every job well helps us live a meaningful and fruitful life.

exercises.title: Daily Work
exercises.instructions: Is the sentence true or false? Use Chapter 8.
exercises.question: Yunus says that only big and important jobs need to be done well.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 8 says: “Every job is important, so we should do it well and correctly for the love of Allah.”

feedback.correct: Correct! For Yunus, every job is important, even a simple one like carrying wood.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 8 again. Which jobs does Yunus say are important?

languageFocusExercises.title: Must or Should?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the two lines. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: A: “Our hearts must be full of love for Him …” B: “… we should do it well and correctly …” Which word gives the stronger rule?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Must” is strong: It says something is necessary. “Should” is softer: It gives good advice. Both come before the base verb: “must be”, “should do”. In “Every job is important, so we should do it well”, “so” shows the result of the first idea.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Must” is stronger than “should”.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 8 again. Think: A school rule says “You must …”; a friend’s advice says “You should …”. Which one is stronger?

languageFocusExercises.title: Yunus’s Message
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match the beginnings and endings to make sentences from Chapter 8.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which ending completes each sentence about Yunus’s message?

matchingPairs.right: to always remember Allah in our hearts
must always do our best when we work
live a meaningful and fruitful life
and let my life end in the hands of a dervish

correctAnswer.Yunus tells us: to always remember Allah in our hearts
correctAnswer.He says that we: must always do our best when we work
correctAnswer.This helps us: live a meaningful and fruitful life
correctAnswer.At least pick me: and let my life end in the hands of a dervish

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Tell + person + to + verb” gives someone’s advice: “Yunus tells us to always remember Allah.” “Help + person + verb” shows a good result: “This helps us live a meaningful life.” “Let + person/thing + verb” asks for permission: “let my life end in the hands of a dervish”.

feedback.correct: Good. You rebuilt the sentences of Yunus’s message.
feedback.incorrect: Read Chapter 8 again. After “tells us”, we need “to”. After “helps us”, we need a verb without “to”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Say It: A Meaningful Daily Life
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Give four short pieces of advice for daily life.
languageFocusExercises.question: How can Yunus’s lesson help you every day?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong A2 response transfers the chapter’s language from the story to a simple personal message about everyday behavior.

feedback.correct: Use the sentence starters to turn the chapter’s language into clear daily-life advice.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Give Yunus’s message: “Yunus tells us to …”
discussionPrompts.example: Yunus tells us to always remember Allah in our hearts.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Give advice and a reason: “We should … because …”
discussionPrompts.example: We should do our homework carefully because every job is important.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Say the result: “This helps us …”
discussionPrompts.example: This helps us live a meaningful and fruitful life.

age.died: Yunus Emre dies. He is about {years} old.

places.name: Anatolia
places.text: Yunus Emre was born in Anatolia in 1240. He died in 1320. Today, Anatolia is a part of Türkiye.
places.teacherNote: Many towns say they have the grave of Yunus Emre. Do not show one place as certain.
places.question: Which country is Anatolia a part of today?

places.name: Konya
places.text: Konya was the capital city of the Anatolian Seljuks. Mevlana lived here and died here in 1273. Yunus Emre lived at the same time.
places.teacherNote: Chapter 1 says Yunus was 33 or 34 years old when Mevlana died.
places.question: How old was Yunus Emre in 1273? Move the slider to check.

places.name: Kösedağ, 1243
places.text: In 1243, the Anatolian Seljuk army fought the Mongol army here. The Anatolian Seljuks lost. After that, life in Anatolia became very hard. Yunus Emre was only three years old.
places.teacherNote: The exact battlefield is not known. Sources place it near Kösedağ, about 80 km northeast of Sivas. The B1 and B2 books tell this event in detail.
places.question: What happened in Anatolia after 1243?

places.name: Syria
places.text: Yunus Emre traveled to Syria. Big cities like Aleppo and Damascus were there.
places.teacherNote: In the 13th century, Syria (al-Sham) was a larger region than the country today.
places.question: Which two big cities can you see in Syria?

places.name: Azerbaijan
places.text: Yunus Emre also traveled to Azerbaijan. At that time, Azerbaijan was the land around the city of Tabriz. The Mongol army came to Anatolia from here.
places.teacherNote: Medieval Azerbaijan is mostly in north-west Iran today. It is not the same as the modern Republic of Azerbaijan.
places.question: Which army came to Anatolia from this land?

challenge.prompt: Find Anatolia, the home of Yunus Emre.

exercises.title: Easy to Understand
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer.
exercises.question: Why could people easily understand Yunus Emre’s poems?
options: He wrote and said them in simple Turkish.
He wrote them only for madrasa students.
He wrote them in Syria and Azerbaijan.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 1: “People could easily understand his poems because he wrote and said them in simple Turkish.”

feedback.correct: Yes! He used simple Turkish, so everyone could understand his poems. This also helped the Turkish language.
feedback.incorrect: Not this one. Read the first paragraph of Chapter 1 again. Find the word “because”.

exercises.title: Bad Habits
exercises.instructions: Read the sentence. Is it true or false?
exercises.question: Dervishes tried to keep habits like jealousy and gossiping.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 2: “They always tried to leave bad habits like jealousy, arrogance, stinginess, greediness, selfishness, or gossiping.”

feedback.correct: Right, it is false. Jealousy and gossiping are bad habits, and dervishes always tried to leave them.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last sentence of Chapter 2 again. What did dervishes try to do with bad habits?

exercises.title: A Dervish Without a Tongue
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer.
exercises.question: The poem says a dervish must be “tongueless” when people make fun of him. What does this mean?
options: He makes fun of them, too.
He does not answer them back.
He cries with eyes full of tears.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 3: “He must be tongueless when people make fun of him.”

feedback.correct: Yes. He has a tongue, but he stays quiet. He does not answer bad words with bad words.
feedback.incorrect: Not this one. Read the second part of the poem in Chapter 3. What does a person do with his tongue?

exercises.title: Why Cut Wood?
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer.
exercises.question: Taptuk gave Yunus ordinary work like cutting wood. What was the main goal of this work?
options: to collect the most wood on the mountain
to make him strong for his travels
to break his ego and give up bad habits
exercises.explanation: Chapter 4: “Some jobs look ordinary at first glance. The primary goal is to break the ego and give up bad habits.”

feedback.correct: Yes! The work looked ordinary, but its real goal was to make Yunus a better person inside.
feedback.incorrect: Not this one. Read the second paragraph of Chapter 4 again. Find the words “The primary goal”.

exercises.title: Taptuk Watches Yunus
exercises.instructions: Read the sentence. Is it true or false?
exercises.question: Taptuk Emre never noticed what kind of wood Yunus brought.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 5: “Taptuk Emre noticed that Yunus never carried crooked wood to the house.”

feedback.correct: Right, it is false. Taptuk noticed that Yunus never brought crooked wood, so he asked him why.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 5 again. What did Taptuk Emre notice?

exercises.title: Learning from Nature
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer.
exercises.question: What did Yunus do when he looked at nature?
options: He found a lesson in everything in it.
He picked every flower that he saw.
He looked only for straight wood.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 6: “He looked at nature and found a lesson from everything in it, like reading the Qur’an.”

feedback.correct: Yes! For Yunus, nature was like a book. Everything in it taught him something.
feedback.incorrect: Not this one. Read the second paragraph of Chapter 6 again. What did Yunus find in nature?

exercises.title: The Flower Task
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer.
exercises.question: What did Taptuk Emre promise to the student with the most beautiful bunch of flowers?
options: He would take that student to Syria.
He would give that student a gift.
He would give him the wood-cutting duties.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 7: “I will give a gift to whoever prepares the most beautiful bunch of flowers.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Taptuk promised a gift, so all the dervishes ran to the fields to pick flowers.
feedback.incorrect: Not this one. Read Taptuk’s words at the start of Chapter 7 again.

exercises.title: The Daisy’s Wish
exercises.instructions: Read the sentence. Is it true or false?
exercises.question: The daisy wanted its life to end in the hands of a dervish.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 8: “At least pick me and let my life end in the hands of a dervish.”

feedback.correct: Right, it is true. The daisy was dying, so it asked Yunus to pick it. It wanted to end its life with a dervish.
feedback.incorrect: Read the daisy’s words at the start of Chapter 8 again. What did the daisy ask Yunus to do?

exercises.title: Look: Two Kinds of Past
exercises.instructions: Look at the past verb. Put each sentence in the right group.
exercises.question: How does each verb show the past?

items: He traveled to many cities in Anatolia …
Yunus served his teacher Taptuk Emre …
The students whispered in each other’s ears …
… found a lesson from everything in it.
All the dervishes went out into the fields.

The verb adds -ed: He traveled to many cities in Anatolia …
Yunus served his teacher Taptuk Emre …
The students whispered in each other’s ears …
The verb changes (no -ed): … found a lesson from everything in it.
All the dervishes went out into the fields.

exercises.explanation: The book tells Yunus’s story in the past. Many verbs add -ed: travel → traveled, serve → served, whisper → whispered. Some verbs change and do not take -ed: tell → told, find → found, go → went. Learn these past forms one by one.

feedback.correct: Well done. You found the -ed verbs and the verbs that change.
feedback.incorrect: Say the verb today (travel, tell, go …). Does the past form only add -ed, or does it change?

exercises.title: Look: How Often? How Many?
exercises.instructions: Match each phrase from the book with its meaning.
exercises.question: What do always, never, a single and some mean?

matchingPairs.left: he never cut or brought green or crooked wood
he returned with a single daisy
Some dervishes were making fun of Yunus.
matchingPairs.right: part of a group, not all of them

part of a group, not all of them

exercises.explanation: “Always” and “never” tell us how often: always = at all times, never = not one time. “A single” and “some” tell us how many: A single = only one, some = a part of the group. These small words make a story exact.

feedback.correct: Correct. Always and never tell us how often. A single and some tell us how many.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the small word in each sentence: always, never, a single, some. Is it about time or about number?

exercises.title: Look: It Looks Like …
exercises.instructions: Read the sentences. Then choose the best answer.
exercises.question: Chapter 4: “Some jobs look ordinary at first glance.” Chapter 5: “It looked like Yunus was working with wood to fix crooked pieces. But in fact, he was training his own heart and ego.” What do “look” and “It looked like” tell us?
exercises.explanation: “Look” and “It looked like …” tell us what we see at first. “But in fact …” then tells us what is really true: The work looks like wood-cutting, but it trains Yunus’s heart.

feedback.correct: Correct. “It looked like” is the first picture. “But in fact” gives the real meaning.
feedback.incorrect: Read Chapter 5 again. Which words come first: what we see, or what is true?

exercises.title: Practise: Reason, Result, Different Idea
exercises.instructions: Fill the gaps from the word bank. Two words are not needed.
exercises.question: Which word fits each gap?
exercises.fillBlanksText: People could easily understand his poems [blank] he wrote and said them in simple Turkish. … Dervishes were fully aware that they were in need of Allah in every way. [blank], even if they were rich, they always called themselves poor. … they could call themselves poor, [blank] their hearts were very rich. … Every job is important, [blank] we should do it well and correctly …
exercises.explanation: “Because” + a sentence gives a reason. “That is why” and “so” give a result: First the reason, then what happens. “But” gives a different idea: Poor, but rich hearts. “Because of” needs a noun after it (“because of the Creator”), not a sentence.

feedback.correct: Well done. You linked reasons, results and different ideas.
feedback.incorrect: For each gap, ask: Does the next part give a reason, a result, or a different idea? Check Chapter 1, Chapter 2 and the end of Chapter 8.

exercises.title: Practise: What Comes After the Verb?
exercises.instructions: Choose the correct form for each sentence from the book.
exercises.question: What comes after “taught him how”, “helped him” and “let my life”?

formChoices.sentence: This service taught him how [choice] a good heart and do the right thing.
For Yunus, woodcutting in nature helped him [choice] a better person.
At least pick me and let my life [choice] in the hands of a dervish.

exercises.explanation: After “how”, use “to + verb”: “taught him how to have”. After “help + person” and “let + person/thing”, use the base verb: “helped him become”, “let my life end”.

feedback.correct: Correct. How + to + verb; help and let + base verb.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the verb before the gap: taught … how, helped …, let …. Check Chapters 5, 6 and 8.

exercises.title: Practise: Fix One Mistake
exercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
exercises.question: Can you fix the verb in each sentence?

errorItems.sentence: He choosed the straightest pieces of wood with the greatest care.
They picked flowers and runned back to their teacher.
He says that we must to always do our best when we work.

exercises.explanation: “Choose” and “run” change in the past: chose, ran (not choosed, runned). After “must”, use the base verb without “to”: “we must always do our best”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You fixed all three sentences.
feedback.incorrect: Compare with the book: Chapter 5 (the straightest pieces), Chapter 7 (the flowers) and Chapter 8 (do our best).

exercises.title: Practise: Every Time …
exercises.instructions: Put the words in order to make the sentence from Chapter 5.
exercises.question: What changed each time Yunus worked?
exercises.explanation: “Every time + action” means: again and again, each time this happens. “Make + something + adjective” shows a change: A bad part becomes better. Chapter 6 uses the same pattern: “Yunus made his heart purer.”

feedback.correct: Well done. Every time … shows a repeated action, and made … better shows the change.
feedback.incorrect: Start with the time words “Every time”. Then say what he did, and what he made better.

exercises.title: Use: A Helper at School
exercises.instructions: Fill the gaps in this new text. Two words are not needed.
exercises.question: Can you use the book’s words in a school story?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Mrs Ayşe works in our school kitchen. [blank] day, she cooks lunch for many students. She [blank] comes late. It looks like an easy job, [blank] in fact it is hard work. [blank], we always say “thank you” to her.
exercises.explanation: “Every day” shows a daily habit. “Never” means not one time. “It looks like …, but in fact …” gives the first picture and then the truth. “That is why” gives the result. Like Yunus’s story, the text says that ordinary work is important.

feedback.correct: Well done. You used the book’s language in a new place.
feedback.incorrect: Ask for each gap: How often? what we see or what is true? a reason or a result?

exercises.title: Use: An Everyday Hero
exercises.instructions: Write 4–5 sentences about a helper. Tell a partner first.
exercises.question: Who helps others every day in your life?
exercises.explanation: Example: “Mr Ali is our school caretaker. Every day, he opens the doors at seven. It looks like an easy job, but in fact he works very hard. Last winter, he fixed the heater in our classroom. His job is important, so we should keep our school clean. This helps us study well.”

feedback.correct: Check your sentences: past verbs, how often, It looks like … but in fact …, so, should, helps us.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Say how often: “Every day, he/she …” or “He/She never …”
discussionPrompts.example: Every day, our school cleaner opens the classrooms early, and she never comes late.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Give one past event: “Last week, he/she …”
discussionPrompts.example: Last week, she helped a small boy find his lost bag.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Say how it looks and what is true: “It looks like …, but in fact …”
discussionPrompts.example: It looks like her job is easy, but in fact it is very hard work.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Give the result: “His/Her job is important, so we should … . This helps us …”
discussionPrompts.example: Her job is important, so we should keep our classrooms clean. This helps us study well.

pages.title: Final Challenge
pages.content: Bring the whole story together in the Final Challenge.

exercises.title: Schools in Yunus’s Time
exercises.instructions: Complete the sentence from Chapter 1 with one word: madrasas, mosques or markets.
exercises.question: What were schools called at that time?
exercises.fillBlanksText: At that time, schools were called [blank].
exercises.explanation: Chapter 1 says: “At that time, schools were called madrasas. After he completed his madrasa education, he followed the way of the dervishes and became a dervish.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Yunus first studied at a madrasa and then chose the way of the dervishes.
feedback.incorrect: Read the start of the second paragraph of Chapter 1.

exercises.title: Poems for Today
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer.
exercises.question: Why are Yunus Emre’s poems still important for Turkish culture today?
options: They are written in a very old and difficult language.
They tell the history of the Anatolian cities.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 1 says: “His poems have important moral lessons. These lessons are still very important for Turkish culture today.”

feedback.correct: Yes. The lessons in his poems are still alive today.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first paragraph of Chapter 1. What do his poems have?

exercises.title: How the Dervishes Behaved
exercises.instructions: Is the sentence true or false?
exercises.question: The dervishes were often cold and sulky with other people.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 2 says: “They were kind and cheerful; they were not cold or sulky. They tried to understand everyone and found a solution to their problems.”

feedback.correct: Right. The dervishes were kind and cheerful, and they tried to understand everyone.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 2. How did the dervishes treat people?

exercises.title: A Poem About a Hard Path
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer.
exercises.question: Yunus Emre wrote a poem that begins with “You cannot be a dervish.” What does this poem show?
options: The path of dervishhood was very difficult.
Every person can become a dervish in one day.
Dervishes did not like to write poems.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 3 says: “In fact, the path of dervishhood was a very difficult one.” Yunus says this in his poem that begins with the words “You cannot be a dervish.”

feedback.correct: Yes. The poem lists hard things a dervish must do, so the path was not easy.
feedback.incorrect: Read the sentences just before the poem in Chapter 3.

exercises.title: The First Condition
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer.
exercises.question: What was the first condition to be a student in Taptuk Emre’s dervish house?
options: to know many long poems by heart
to come from a rich and famous family
to be humble and ready to serve others
exercises.explanation: Chapter 4 says: “In Taptuk Emre’s dervish house, the first condition to be a student was to be humble and willing to serve people and all creatures.”

feedback.correct: Yes. A student had to be humble and ready to serve people and all living things.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first paragraph of Chapter 4.

exercises.title: Word Meanings
exercises.instructions: Match each word with its meaning in the story.
exercises.question: What does each word mean?

matchingPairs.right: not too much and not too little

correctAnswer.moderate: not too much and not too little

exercises.explanation: Chapter 2: “Dervishes were generous-hearted and open-handed.” Chapter 3: “Dervishes lived a moderate and disciplined life according to Islam.” Chapter 5: “Taptuk Emre noticed that Yunus never carried crooked wood to the house.” Chapter 8: “This helps us live a meaningful and fruitful life.”

feedback.correct: Yes. You found the meaning of each word from its sentence.
feedback.incorrect: Read each word in its sentence in Chapters 2, 3, 5 and 8.

exercises.title: Alone with Allah
exercises.instructions: Is the sentence true or false?
exercises.question: Yunus first learned to be alone with Allah in the mountains.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 6 says: “He first learned to be alone with Allah in the mountains. The mountains are quiet and far from people.”

feedback.correct: True. The quiet mountains helped Yunus think about Allah.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 6. Where did Yunus first learn this?

exercises.title: Who Said It?
exercises.instructions: Match each speaker with their words.
exercises.question: Who said these words?

matchingPairs.right: “Crooked wood cannot go into the dervish house.”
“Today, all of you go up the mountain and bring me flowers.”
“Just look at him! All he could find was a single daisy!”
“My time is up now; I’m dried up and dying.”

correctAnswer.Yunus: “Crooked wood cannot go into the dervish house.”
correctAnswer.Taptuk Emre: “Today, all of you go up the mountain and bring me flowers.”
correctAnswer.Some dervishes: “Just look at him! All he could find was a single daisy!”
correctAnswer.The daisy: “My time is up now; I’m dried up and dying.”

exercises.explanation: Chapter 4: Yunus always said: “Crooked wood cannot go into the dervish house.” Chapter 7: Taptuk Emre said to his students, “Today, all of you go up the mountain and bring me flowers.” The dervishes whispered, “Just look at him! All he could find was a single daisy!” Chapter 8: the daisy says, “My time is up now; I’m dried up and dying.”

feedback.correct: Yes. You remembered who said each sentence.
feedback.incorrect: Look again at Chapters 4, 7 and 8.

exercises.title: Back from the Fields
exercises.instructions: Complete the sentence from Chapter 7 with one word: last, first or second.
exercises.question: When did Yunus come back from the fields?
exercises.explanation: Chapter 7 says: “They picked flowers and ran back to their teacher. Yunus was the last to return. In the late afternoon, he returned with a single daisy.”

feedback.correct: Yes. The others ran back quickly, but Yunus came back late with one daisy.
feedback.incorrect: Read the end of the first paragraph of Chapter 7.

exercises.title: Yunus’s Path
exercises.instructions: Put these events in the order of the story.
exercises.question: What happened first, next and last?

sequencingItems.text: Taptuk asks why Yunus always brings straight wood.
Yunus returns with a single daisy.
Yunus serves his teacher for forty years.
Taptuk sends his students to bring flowers.

exercises.explanation: The madrasa (Chapter 1), forty years of service (Chapter 5), Taptuk’s question (Chapter 5), the flower task (Chapter 7) and the single daisy (Chapter 7).

feedback.correct: Yes. Yunus studied, served for many years, and then learned through the wood and the flowers.
feedback.incorrect: Remember that Taptuk asked about the wood after Yunus had served for forty years.
